source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Code simulates question-answer trees, scores each question by expected information gain over a candidate set, and picks the best one. Beats direct prompting and tree-of-thoughts in 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Abstract: 38.1% average gain in success rate over direct prompting across several LLMs. Llama3-70B open set: 20Q Things 15.5 -> 21.0; DX diagnosis 26.0 -> 35.6; MedDG 25.7 -> 50.6; FloDial troubleshooting 11.1 -> 26.1 (success %).
quote: improves the success rate of multiple LLMs by 38.1%
limits: Needs a closed or enumerable candidate set to compute entropy; open-set results use the model's own candidate lists. Answerer is simulated by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S7: code computes entropy over surviving candidates and picks the splitting probe; the model only proposes and answers.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (closed-set vs open-set and easy vs hard)
finding: Gains are large when candidate outcomes are enumerated (closed set) and in diagnosis-like tasks, but small on easy 20Q sets. Boundary condition: the benefit depends on how well the candidate set is known.
numbers: Llama3-70B Common 20Q: DP 34.2 -> UoT 36.9 (open), 51.4 -> 55.9 (closed); DX closed set 83.7 -> 90.4; Mistral-Large FloDial closed 14.2 -> 30.1. Mean questions in successes fall, e.g. DX closed 3.5 -> 1.0.
limits: Success rates for the weaker 20Q sets stay low (Things 15 to 25%).
agent_relevance: Expect a small gain when the hypothesis set is small or the plain model already splits well; budget the entropy code for cases with real ambiguity.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (equal-compute comparison)
finding: At matched token cost, pruned UoT still beats tree-of-thoughts and other baselines. Deepening adapted-ToT to D=4 to match UoT's cost still leaves it behind UoT at D=3.
numbers: Section 3.3.1 and Table 2: compared on 20Q, medical diagnosis, troubleshooting with GPT-4 token use equalised; exact bars read from a figure.
limits: Authors' own baseline adaptations (heuristic to halve the search space) were added to ToT.
agent_relevance: Supports G7: an information-gain scoring step wins at equal tokens, not only at more tokens.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (reward ablation, Table 3)
finding: Rival reward functions give almost the same result. Information gain (IG) is not clearly better than simple uncertainty-reduction or split-style rewards. Competing explanation: the structure of the lookahead tree, not the entropy formula, does most of the work.
numbers: GPT-3.5 success % on 20Q-BIG-bench / Common / DX / MedDG / FloDial: IG 51.7/41.4/90.4/81.1/67.9; UR (their final reward) 51.7/44.2/92.1/81.3/67.1; PFS 37.9/36.9/89.4/81.3/67.1.
limits: Single model, differences of 1 to 3 points are inside noise; PFS is clearly worse only on 20Q-BIG-bench (37.9).
agent_relevance: Do not over-invest in the exact entropy formula. Any rule that scores how evenly a probe splits the candidates is probably enough.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) Probing the Multi-turn Planning Capabilities of LLMs via 20 Question Games
finding: Plain LLMs are poor at choosing informative yes/no questions. Even GPT-4 wins only one third (Things) to one half (Celebrities) of games in up to 20 turns. A typical failure is early enumeration: guessing specific items before narrowing the space.
numbers: Success (5 runs x 30 items): GPT-4 0.31 Things, 0.50 Celebrities; GPT-3.5 0.28/0.27; Claude-2 0.21/0.31; Vicuna 7B 0.09/0.06. Judge error 3.07% and 2.95%.
limits: Judge is an LLM; items drawn from model-known entities; older models.
agent_relevance: Baseline for probe choice without a scaffold: plain models waste turns on guesses. Gives a reason for a rule that forbids guessing before the candidate set is small.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) 20 Question Games (training interventions)
finding: Imitating GPT-4 on 600 games helps a small model, and imitating only the successful games helps more than imitating all games. Reinforcement from self-play also helps in-domain but transfers weakly.
numbers: Things success: Vicuna 7B 0.09 -> fine-tuned on all games 0.13 -> successes only 0.23; Vicuna 13B 0.18 -> 0.21 (all) / 0.25 (success); RL self-play 7B 0.26, 13B 0.27. Celebrities (out of domain): V-FT 7B (Suc.) 0.15, RL 7B 0.16 (vs 0.06 base).
limits: Training, not scaffolding. Gains on out-of-domain Celebrities are small and uneven.
agent_relevance: Questioning skill is learnable but narrow; a code-level selector generalises across domains better than a trained habit.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) 20 Question Games (failure mode and reasoner/guesser split)
finding: Most of the planning gain comes from the questioning model: pairing a weak Vicuna 7B reasoner with GPT-4 only barely helps, while a stronger planner helps a lot. Rival explanation (knowledge limit) is weakened.
numbers: Section 6 text: Vicuna 7B as reasoner with GPT-4 as planner shows little improvement over Vicuna 7B alone; GPT-4 planner gives significant improvement. Exact scores not copied.
limits: Exact numbers for this table were not extracted; read qualitatively.
agent_relevance: The weak step is choosing the question, not knowing the answers; this is where code selection pays.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Sample candidate solutions from the model, then choose the clarifying question that best splits those candidates (expected information gain over solution space), instead of letting the model reason about which question is good. Large gains on code generation with hidden requirements.
numbers: HumanEval (48 tasks, 3x3 seeds), accuracy after 4 questions, GPT-3.5 binary: 70.8 -> 85.6; open: 75.9 -> 85.0. Llama3-8B binary 53.0 -> 65.8; open 64.8 -> 75.5. APPS (47 tasks) GPT-4o-mini open 75.1 -> 87.2; Llama3-8B open 39.2 -> 50.7.
limits: Needs an answer model that can score each candidate solution under each answer; simulated user.
agent_relevance: Best-matched evidence for S7: reason in the space of candidate answers, not the space of questions.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation (strong-model boundary)
finding: The stronger the base model, the smaller the gain from entropy-based question choice. Boundary condition on effect size.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-4o-mini, 4 questions: binary 79.6 vs 81.5 EIG; open 83.5 vs 83.8 (gap about 2 and 0.3 points) while GPT-3.5 gap is about 15 and 9 points. Zero-question accuracy GPT-4o-mini 71.0 vs GPT-3.5 44.1.
quote: for more capable models, the gap between the baseline questioning strategies and their EIG-equivalent version is smaller
limits: Part of the strong model's base accuracy is already high, so there is less left to disambiguate.
agent_relevance: Gate the entropy step by need: use it when candidates still disagree, skip when the plain model is already consistent.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation (20 Questions, probability source)
finding: Where the probabilities come from matters. Using the LLM's own log-probs over candidates to score information gain (EIG-logprobs) is much worse than a uniform weighting over sampled candidates (EIG-uniform). The paper blames a poorly biased LLM generative distribution.
numbers: Rank score after 10 questions (higher better): Llama3-70B EIG-uniform 6.3, EIG-logprobs 3.9, implicit 5.9, implicit-ToT 5.1; GPT-3.5 EIG-uniform 6.2, logprobs 4.1, implicit 4.9. GPT-4o-mini gap shrinks (6.8 vs 5.5 implicit). Setup: 15 animals, 5 run seeds, 25 eval seeds.
limits: Note that for Llama3-70B plain implicit reasoning (5.9) is close to EIG-uniform (6.3) at t=10; early turns show the larger gap (t=1: 1.3 vs 0.5).
agent_relevance: G5: do not trust model probabilities as the weights. Count distinct sampled candidates in code and treat them as equal-weight.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation (binary vs open questions)
finding: Open questions (many possible answers) carry more information than yes/no, as theory predicts, but cost the answerer more effort.
numbers: APPS GPT-4o-mini after 4 questions: base binary 62.9, EIG binary 75.3, base open 75.1, EIG open 87.2. Llama3-8B: EIG binary 26.9 vs EIG open 50.7.
limits: Simulated answerers; open questions are easy for a simulated user.
agent_relevance: When the oracle is a program (test run), prefer probes with many distinguishable outcomes, such as printing a value, over pass/fail probes.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2023/2024) Active Preference Inference using Language Models and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Plain instruction-tuned LLMs ask relevant but low-information questions. A probabilistic model whose conditionals are LLM calls, with questions chosen by expected entropy or expected model change, does better on a shopping task with fewer user turns.
numbers: Entropy-reduction LLM beats both baselines once more than one question is allowed (binary and soft reward, Figure 2). Exact values only in figures.
limits: Short workshop paper; closed set of candidate questions; assumes a binary-reward user model; soft reward result holds despite mismatch.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as b01 and b08, from an independent group: LLM defines the distributions, code does the argmax.

source: Li, Belinda Z., Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Choosing the single missing variable to ask about is hard for LLMs even when they can solve the fully specified problem. Large gap between math and logic or planning.
numbers: Accuracy over frontier and open models (March 2025): over 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q; only 40 to 50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Four domains, multiple-choice question, at most one question needed.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple-choice format; 1-sufficient problems only; math may be over-trained.
agent_relevance: Do not assume reasoning ability gives probe-choice ability. Probe choice needs its own code check, for example by backward search over the dependency graph.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench (difficulty axes and detection)
finding: Accuracy drops with number of variables, constraints and search depth (moderate negative Spearman correlations, strongest in Logic-Q and Planning-Q). Models are also poor at noticing that a problem is underspecified at all.
numbers: Spearman values mostly -0.1 to -0.3, some Planning-Q axes near -0.5 (Table 3). Underspecification detection F1 is low for most LLMs (Table 7, not copied).
limits: Correlational; the table text was garbled in extraction so only ranges are given.
agent_relevance: Probe choice degrades with search depth, which is the case where code-level search over the causal graph is most useful.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench (search baseline)
finding: A plain breadth-first search to a fixed depth is a reference solver that solves 1-sufficient problems, and its runtime tracks what makes problems hard for the models. This argues that the needed probe can be computed.
numbers: Section 5.2: difficulty axes include brute-force expected number of guesses and backward search depth; depth-3/5/10 BFS rows rise from partial to near 100% on the easy domains (table text partly garbled).
limits: Exact BFS numbers not recovered.
agent_relevance: The probe in toy structures can be computed rather than asked of the model.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling (CogSci 2024)
finding: Sample k questions from an LLM, translate each to a program, score by expected information gain on the board state, ask the best. With small k the system matches human informativeness. Raw single LLM questions are noisy.
numbers: Human data: 40 participants, 605 question-board pairs, 18 boards. Mean human EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61, 97% of human questions informative. Single sample (k=1) from CodeLlama/GPT-4 mean EIG about 0.65 to 0.66. k=5 approaches the human mean; k=10 above it (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4); all fall short of best humans.
limits: Needs a program translation and a board simulator; one game.
agent_relevance: Sample-and-select with code scoring is cheap: about 5 to 10 candidate probes are enough to reach average human level.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS (grounding failure of pure LLMs)
finding: Without the code scorer, LLMs do not ground questions in the current board state. GPT-4V given a board image does no better than GPT-4 given no board at all. Few-shot examples help.
numbers: Figure 3 top right: GPT-4 with textual, visual, or no board give similar EIG; few-shot universally increases EIG.
limits: Only EIG averages in a figure; one model family tested with images.
agent_relevance: An LLM asked for the best test may produce a generically plausible test that ignores the actual state. Needs an explicit check that the probe separates live suspects.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS (human question diversity)
finding: Human question type mix differs from LLM proposals, and the LLM proposal distribution is skewed to certain types; code selection corrects the quality but the type mix still follows the prior.
numbers: Figure 4: proportions of Boolean, Color, Location, Number, Orientation, Set questions differ between human, grammar and LLM proposals (e.g. one condition 54.0% Boolean).
limits: Percentages read from a figure; not all slices could be tied to conditions.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit diversity requirement to the proposal step so that the high-gain probe types appear among candidates.

source: Golovin and Krause (2011/2017) Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization
finding: For objectives with adaptive monotone submodularity, the greedy adaptive policy is near optimal. Generalised binary search (the Bayesian half-split on probability mass) is shown to be a special case. Greedy is therefore provably not far from optimal for sequential noiseless testing.
numbers: Greedy gets at least (1-1/e) of the best policy for fixed-budget maximisation. Generalised binary search with uniform prior: at most (ln(|H|-1)+1)^2 times the optimal expected queries (Theorem 13 applied). Older results: O(log|H|) worst case (Arkin 1993), O(log 1/min p) expected (Kosaraju 1999, Dasgupta 2004).
limits: Noise-free tests are assumed in the main result; noisy tests only with extra assumptions (persistent noise). Authors retracted an earlier claim for the independent cascade with myopic feedback (counterexample).
agent_relevance: Theoretical reason that picking the probe with greatest expected split each time is acceptable, with only a logarithmic loss against the optimum.

source: Golovin and Krause (2017) Adaptive Submodularity (cost-weighted and noisy settings)
finding: With non-uniform test costs the greedy rule must use gain per unit cost and the guarantee keeps a logarithmic factor; with noisy outcomes the guarantees weaken and need persistent-noise models.
numbers: Interactive submodular set cover with non-uniform costs: logarithmic approximation in the noisy case (Section 13.3); greedy still holds a ln(Q)+1 style factor for integral objectives.
limits: Bound is worst case and could be loose in practice; real tests often violate the independence assumptions.
agent_relevance: For a cost-aware probe selector use gain divided by cost, and expect weaker guarantees when test outputs can mislead.

source: Rainforth, Foster, Ivanova, Bickford Smith (2024) Modern Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Expected information gain is doubly intractable in general, and estimators are expensive. Nested Monte Carlo cannot beat an error rate of O(C^-2/3) in total cost C for most problems, against O(C^-1/2) for unnested.
numbers: EIG estimator cost C = N x M; rate O(C^-2/3) for nested MC; the review lists debiasing and variational routes.
limits: Continuous parameter models mainly; in discrete small hypothesis sets the sum is exact and cheap.
agent_relevance: For our small candidate sets the exact entropy sum is cheap; do not bring in heavy estimators.

source: Rainforth et al. (2024) Modern Bayesian Experimental Design (greedy is suboptimal; learned policies)
finding: Step-by-step greedy design is subtly suboptimal because it ignores effects on later steps. Learned design policies (deep adaptive design) gave better decisions than greedy in several reported studies, partly through non-myopic planning and avoiding approximate inference errors.
numbers: No single effect size is given in the review; cited studies are [13, 42, 73].
limits: Learned policies need training and a simulator; not applicable to a scaffold without training.
agent_relevance: Rival to greedy probes: lookahead of 2 steps in code may help when probes interact (UoT does a limited-depth lookahead).

source: Rainforth et al. (2024) Modern Bayesian Experimental Design (misspecification)
finding: Entropy-driven design can fail badly when the model is wrong, because the same model both fits the data and picks the data. Failure case: stuck querying similar designs. For linear regression, EIG always prefers the extreme inputs, so the interior is never tested.
numbers: No numbers; references [17, 37, 58, 81, 85, 162].
quote: BAD becomes stuck querying similar designs, producing poor-quality datasets
limits: Qualitative review claim.
agent_relevance: Guard (G3): when the hypothesis space may be missing the true cause, add a probe chosen from outside the model (random or mutation check). Links to Anomaly handling and fixation.

source: Nori, Horvitz et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: On 304 NEJM cases, off-the-shelf models trade accuracy for test cost. An orchestrator with explicit hypothesis tracking, an adversarial challenger and a cost steward reaches higher accuracy at much lower cost than the same model alone.
numbers: o3 alone 78.6% at $7,850 per case; MAI-DxO (no budget) 81.9% at $4,735; budget setting 79.9% at $2,396; ensembling 85.5% at $7,184. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. Average gain 11 points across model families.
limits: Gatekeeper is an LLM that invents findings for tests not in the case; NEJM cases are hard teaching cases; components were bundled so the value of information scoring alone is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence of cost-weighted probing with LLMs: structured hypothesis tracking plus a cost check beats a bare model on the cost-accuracy frontier.

source: Nori, Horvitz et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis (physician comparison and failure of plain models)
finding: Physicians scored low; the baseline model ordered reasonable tests rather than tests that most reduced uncertainty per dollar, and anchored on first impressions. The orchestrator forced the question of whether the same information could be had more cheaply.
numbers: Physicians: 19.9% accuracy at $2,963 per case, 764 diagnoses over 56 cases, average 36 cases each, 11.8 min, 6.6 questions, 7.2 tests. Best physician 41%. Weaker models did a false economy, considering fewer differentials and never ordering the confirming tests.
quote: lack a theory of information value
limits: Physician sample from US and UK, median 12 years experience; physicians evaluated on the 56 held-out cases only; qualitative case reading.
agent_relevance: Two named failure modes to guard: ordering tests that confirm the current hypothesis, and under-testing because only few suspects were listed.

source: Nori, Horvitz et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis (memorization and robustness checks)
finding: The 56 most recent cases were held out to check memorization, and results hold on that set. Compute cost per case is tiny against test cost.
numbers: Model inference about $0.15 per case; MAI-DxO showed comparable absolute performance on training and test splits. Agents tend to score higher on the 56-case test set than on all 304.
limits: Cases are behind a paywall but could still be partly in training data.
agent_relevance: Test costs dominate in clinical settings, but for our agent the probe cost is tokens or wall time, so cost weights must be rescaled.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: LLMs prompted to ask the most informative open-ended or yes/no question, or to generate edge cases, learn user preferences faster than users writing prompts or labelling examples chosen by pool-based active learning. Significance only in two of three domains.
numbers: 388 participants: 183 content recommendation, 121 moral reasoning, 84 email validation; 6 elicitation methods. Metric: area under p(correct) vs interaction time. Significant over baselines in content recommendation and email validation, not in moral reasoning. Average preference variation 0.77 bits.
limits: The prompt only says generate the most informative question; no explicit entropy computation. AUROC metric shows weaker and more variable gains (miscalibration).
agent_relevance: Prompted informativeness alone gives some gain on human tasks, but the sound evidence for gains is domain specific.

source: Li et al. (2023) GATE (effort and moderators)
finding: Users found interactive elicitation less mentally demanding than writing prompts and said it surfaced considerations they had not thought of. Open-ended generative questions did best in content recommendation.
numbers: Mental demand ratings: labelling and yes/no methods lower than prompting (Figure 4 left); values in figure.
limits: Self-report, Prolific participants; instructions told participants not to follow the transcript if it clashed with their intuition and compliance was not verified.
agent_relevance: Moderator: question format matters, open-ended questions give more information; the cost of answering also differs.

source: Beck, Sivasubramanian, Dani, Ramakrishnan, Iyer (2021) Effective Evaluation of Deep Active Learning on Image Classification Tasks
finding: A unified re-run of active learning methods finds active learning does give label savings over random sampling, but the extra value of sophisticated selection over plain uncertainty sampling vanishes once data augmentation is used. Batch size and seed-set choice matter little.
numbers: AL is 2x to 4x more label-efficient than random sampling when data augmentation is used. With augmentation, BADGE has no consistent gain over simple uncertainty (entropy) sampling. Reasonable batch sizes and seed sets had little to no impact.
limits: Image classification with deep nets, not LLM question asking.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for b04: a simple max-uncertainty rule is often as good as a sophisticated one. Supports keeping S7 simple.

source: Beck et al. (2021) Effective Evaluation of Deep Active Learning (contradictory prior results)
finding: Earlier papers disagreed about whether active learning beats random sampling, mainly because of differences in training setups. Unified re-implementation resolves part of the conflict.
numbers: Abstract: contradictory observations on algorithm performance; unclear scenarios in which AL beats random sampling (RS).
limits: Per-regime numbers not copied; conclusions depend on augmentation and redundancy of data.
agent_relevance: Expect effect sizes of selection methods to depend on the base procedure; always measure against random probe choice.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: Question-Asking LLMs and a Benchmark for Reliable Interactive Clinical Reasoning
finding: Directly prompting strong LLMs to ask questions makes diagnosis worse than giving them the complete case. Abstention logic that decides when to ask recovers part of the loss. Filtering irrelevant context and reformatting the dialogue also help.
numbers: Abstention strategies improve diagnostic accuracy by 22.3% (baseline not given in the abstract). Performance still lags the full-information upper bound.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session; the full-text figures were not available.
agent_relevance: Asking has a downside: bad questions can lower accuracy. The decision to probe at all needs a code gate.

source: de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults. Artificial Intelligence 32
finding: GDE picks the next measurement that minimises the expected entropy of the diagnosis distribution, using a one-step lookahead over the leading candidates. Prior fault probabilities are needed.
numbers: No numbers from memory.
limits: From memory, not opened. Assumes independent component failure priors and a candidate set that includes the true fault.
agent_relevance: The origin of S7 entropy-based probe choice.

source: Heckerman, Breese, Rommelse (1995) Decision-theoretic troubleshooting. Communications of the ACM 38(3)
finding: Troubleshooting under a single-fault assumption: the optimal order for repair or check actions follows probability-to-cost ratio when actions are independent. Applied to printer troubleshooting at Microsoft.
numbers: No numbers from memory.
limits: From memory, not opened. Single fault and conditional independence assumptions; the general problem is hard.
agent_relevance: Cost-weighted probing: rank checks by probability of fixing per unit cost.

source: Hyafil and Rivest (1976) Constructing optimal binary decision trees is NP-complete
finding: Finding the optimal fixed test sequence is NP-complete, so greedy halving or entropy rules are the practical choice.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: From memory, not opened.
agent_relevance: Justifies greedy S7 instead of full planning.

source: Kadane and Simon (1977) Optimal strategies for a class of constrained sequential problems. Annals of Statistics 5
finding: For series-system testing with independent costs, ordering tests by probability over cost gives the optimal strategy. With equal cost and equal probability this reduces to splitting the candidates in half.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: From memory, not opened; the claim relies on a special structure.
agent_relevance: Half-split is the special case of cost-weighted probing when costs and priors are uniform.
